rows.description: A toddler cries hard at loud noises, separation or a changed routine and takes a long time to settle. This is sensitivity of the nervous system, not bad parenting or bad behaviour, and steady comfort helps.
A teenager swings between worry, irritation and low confidence over grades, looks and friends. Puberty amplifies emotion; the pattern is common, and it becomes a concern when it stops daily life.

rows.subtype: Sensitive alarm system as an asset [Actor]
rows.description: A professional who worries a lot also catches risks early, prepares thoroughly and feels for others. Learns that the alarm is useful information, not always a verdict, and builds rest into work.
A toddler claps at a song or an achievement, sharing joy and copying others. Clapping together is a happy social routine.
A preschooler clenches the fists in anger or frustration, an early sign of strong feeling. Adults can offer words for the feeling and safe outlets, such as squeezing a soft ball.

rows.subtype: Clapping and snapping in peer groups [Expressing]
rows.description: A teenager claps or snaps as approval among friends, or slowly claps sarcastically. Tone and speed show whether it is praise or mockery.

rows.subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
rows.description: A student reasons that laws exist to protect everyone's rights and welfare, and that unjust ones should be changed by fair, democratic means, not simply obeyed or broken.
A professional follows the rule in ordinary cases but raises a formal objection when it would harm people, and accepts the outcome of a fair process even when it goes against them.
A toddler pushes away a helping hand, insists on putting on their own shoes and then clings to a parent again minutes later. Both wanting independence and needing safety are true at once.

rows.subtype: Wanting privacy but still needing comfort [Actor]
rows.description: A child begins closing the bedroom door and keeping small secrets, yet still wants a parent close when sick or upset. Autonomy grows alongside, not instead of, attachment.
A student in a hostel far from family feels proud of managing alone and then aches for home cooking and familiar voices. Missing home is not weakness; it shows the bond remains.

rows.subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
rows.description: A teenager watches a grandparent who seems content and another who is bitter, and wonders which path they will take. They do not yet grasp how choices accumulate, but the contrast plants a lasting question.

rows.subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
rows.description: A student imagines being sixty with regrets: a safe job never questioned, words left unsaid to parents. The fear can push them toward paralysing perfectionism or toward acting more honestly now.

A teenager who prides themselves on being brutally honest tells a friend her singing is bad and calls it truth. Bluntness can serve the speaker's need to feel superior more than the listener's growth.
A young adult learns that the same true feedback can be said with care, at the right moment, or as a weapon. Honesty joined with kindness is harder than either alone and lasts longer.
